Subject: Follow-up: QuickCommerce inference pilot — latency & throughput clarifications

Hi Markus,

Thanks for the call today — appreciate the clarity on how Redwood structures pilots. A quick recap from our side and a couple of clarifying questions so we can pick next steps: 

- Production traffic profile (approx): baseline 20 QPS, steady-state 120 QPS during business hours, peak bursts up to ~280 QPS (primarily 30–90s bursts).
- Typical prompt length: median ~45 tokens; 95th percentile ~160 tokens.
- SLA targets: p95 tail latency <120ms for inference (end-to-end from request to token stream start) for our core pricing endpoints; p99 <350ms is a stretch goal.
- Data constraints: customer data is only transient; no long term storage. We need SOC2 evidence and an audit log for the pilot.

Questions:
1) Given the burstiness, do you recommend starting with Hosted API with burst credits or go straight to Dedicated capacity?
2) If Hosted, can you guarantee sustained p95 <150ms at 120 QPS? If Dedicated, what lead time and minimal committed capacity should we plan for?

I've attached our latency profile CSV and will share a sample trace and request schema tomorrow.

Next steps we want: a short decision matrix from you with clear criteria (latency thresholds, QPS ranges, cost knobs) and a proposed pilot timeline.

Thanks — we want to move quickly (targeting a pilot in the next 2–3 weeks).

Best,
Sara Lin
Head of Platform
QuickCommerce Inc

Hi Sara — thanks for the concise summary and for the CSV. Helpful. Per your ask, below is a compact priority matrix plus recommended next steps to decide Hosted vs Dedicated quickly.

Priority matrix (rule-of-thumb):
- Hosted API:
  - Best when sustained QPS < ~80–100 and p95 target >= 150ms, or when you need fastest time-to-value and minimal ops.
  - Pros: instant onboarding, automatic burst handling (subject to credits/policies), no infra commits.
  - Cons: less predictable tail latency under large, sustained bursts; cost per-token higher at scale.

- Dedicated capacity (Reserved GPU pools):
  - Best when sustained QPS >= ~100 with tight p95 targets (<150ms) or predictable high throughput (>200 QPS sustained) where unit economics matter.
  - Pros: consistent latency, isolation, capacity guarantees; autoscaling policies you control.
  - Cons: provisioning lead time, minimum commit/contract, ops handoff for rollout.

- Private (VPC / on-prem):
  - Recommended only for regulated workloads or where data residency + network isolation are required; not necessary for your described transient data case.

Concrete recommendation for QuickCommerce based on your numbers:
- Short-term pilot (2 weeks): start on Hosted API with a focused throughput ramp test. We will run a supervised benchmark that mirrors your peak-burst profile (bursts to 280 QPS) and measure p50/p95/p99. This validates whether Hosted meets your p95 120ms goal under real patterns.
- Contingency plan: if p95 exceeds 150ms consistently at your steady 120 QPS or if cost/QPS trend exceeds agreed threshold, transition to Dedicated. For Dedicated we expect a 2–4 week provisioning and tuning window; minimal initial pool: 4 x A100 (or equivalent) depending on model choice.

Pilot operational asks from QuickCommerce:
1) Provide a 24–48hr request sample and a synthetic test harness (we can use your CSV + traces).
2) Confirm target model (open or curated) and whether embedding/reranking calls are in-scope.
3) Share SOC2 contact for compliance docs; Redwood will provide an SOC2 packet and audit log access for the pilot.

I'll attach our Redwood pilot checklist to make the onboarding steps explicit. If that all sounds good I can loop in Neha (infra) to size Dedicated options in parallel so we don't lose time.

Proposed schedule:
- 2026-09-16: Redwood run initial Hosted ramp test (if we receive traces by 09-15).
- 2026-09-23: Review bench results; decision point to either continue Hosted to production or begin Dedicated provisioning.

Would you like us to schedule a 30-minute bench planning call tomorrow?

Thanks,

--
